t: Minimum Moves to Capture The Queen
o: Rook at (a,b), bishop at (c,d), queen at (e,f). Answer is 1 if either white piece already attacks the queen (with no blocker in between), otherwise 2 — with only three pieces on the board, one piece can always clear the way or reposition so the other captures in a second move. Example 2: both pieces attack (5,2) → 1; example 1 needs 2.
k: Answer ∈ {1, 2}: check direct attacks, else return 2.
Blockers: the other white piece may sit strictly between attacker and queen, invalidating a direct capture.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct attack checks with blocker tests
a.i: Rook attacks if same row or column and the bishop isn't strictly between them. Bishop attacks if on a shared diagonal and the rook isn't strictly between. If neither holds, return 2 (always achievable: move the rook to the queen's row/column away from blockers, then capture).
s: If a == e and bishop not strictly between vertically → 1.
If b == f and bishop not strictly between horizontally → 1.
If |c-e| == |d-f| and rook not strictly between diagonally → 1.

w: The subtle part is the blocker conditions — strictly-between checks (min < x < max, exclusive). Argue why 2 always suffices: the rook can move along its row/column to align with the queen unobstructed in one move (worst case stepping around the bishop), then capture. Enumerative alternative: BFS over states, unnecessary here.
